scenarios.title: Web servers in two data centers
scenarios.situation: You manage web servers in Boston and Austin plus database servers in Boston. You need to target 'all Boston web servers' and 'all web servers everywhere' from one inventory file.
scenarios.prompt: Which INI inventory structure gives you both groupings?
choices: Add [web:children] with boston_web and austin_web, and [boston:children] with boston_web and boston_db
List every host twice under literal [boston] and [web] groups with duplicate entries
Create two separate inventory files — one per data center — and merge them at runtime
Put all hosts in one [all] group and use --limit with regexes for every run
scenarios.why: The :children suffix builds parent groups from child groups without duplicating host entries, so 'web' means every web server and 'boston' means every Boston host. Ansible merges group membership automatically; duplicate entries and split files just create maintenance debt.
scenarios.hint: How do you compose groups out of other groups in INI inventory?

scenarios.title: The config that wouldn't apply
scenarios.situation: You set 'forks = 50' in /etc/ansible.cfg, but runs still use 5 forks. A teammate mentions there's an ansible.cfg in your project directory and ANSIBLE_CONFIG is set in your shell.
scenarios.prompt: Which config actually wins, and where should the project setting live?
choices: ANSIBLE_CONFIG env var wins; then ./ansible.cfg; then ~/.ansible.cfg; then /etc/ansible.cfg — put project settings in ./ansible.cfg
/etc/ansible.cfg always wins as the system-wide config
~/.ansible.cfg wins over everything except the project file
Ansible merges all four files, so forks should have been 50 + 5
scenarios.why: Ansible uses the FIRST config found in this order: ANSIBLE_CONFIG environment variable, ./ansible.cfg (project), ~/.ansible.cfg (user), /etc/ansible.cfg (system). It does not merge files. For a project, ./ansible.cfg is the right home; unset or fix ANSIBLE_CONFIG if it's pointing somewhere stale.
scenarios.hint: Does Ansible merge config files, or pick one?

scenarios.title: The pipe that did nothing remotely
scenarios.situation: You run 'ansible web -m command -a "ps aux | grep nginx"' and get an error about '|' not found. The same pipeline works when you SSH in manually.
scenarios.prompt: Why did the ad hoc command fail, and what's the fix?
choices: The command module runs without a shell, so pipes fail — use -m shell for pipes and redirection
Ansible blocks grep on remote hosts for security — use the find module instead
The pipe needs escaping: ps aux \| grep nginx
Ad hoc commands can't take arguments — write a playbook instead
scenarios.why: The command module executes the binary directly with no shell, so shell metacharacters (|, >, &&) are passed literally as arguments. The shell module wraps the string in /bin/sh -c, enabling pipelines. Rule of thumb: need shell features → shell module; simple binary + args → command module (safer, no shell injection).
scenarios.hint: Which layer interprets the pipe character — the module or a shell?

scenarios.title: Patch Tuesday scoping
scenarios.situation: Your inventory has groups web, db, and cache. Tonight you must patch only the web servers, but skip web3 which is serving a critical batch job.
scenarios.prompt: Which pattern or flag combination targets exactly that set?
choices: ansible-playbook patch.yml --limit 'web:!web3'
ansible-playbook patch.yml --limit web --skip web3
ansible-playbook patch.yml -e target=web (then handle web3 inside the play)
Edit the inventory to delete web3 temporarily
scenarios.why: Patterns support exclusion with '!' — 'web:!web3' means all web hosts except web3. --limit accepts the same pattern language (also '&' for intersection). There is no --skip-hosts flag, and editing inventory for a one-off change is error-prone.
scenarios.hint: What pattern operator removes hosts from a set?

scenarios.title: First-day control node setup
scenarios.situation: You're building a shared Ansible control node. Requirements: use the project's inventory by default, don't prompt on new host keys in this lab, run 20 forks, and escalate privileges with sudo asking for the become password.
scenarios.prompt: Which ansible.cfg settings cover all four?
choices: inventory=./inventory, host_key_checking=False, forks=20, and become=True with become_ask_pass=True
inventory=./inventory, strict_host_key_checking=no, parallel=20, sudo=True
hosts=./inventory, no_host_key_check=1, workers=20, escalate=yes
remote_inventory=./inventory, trust_all_hosts=yes, concurrency=20, root=True
scenarios.why: The real [defaults] keys are inventory, host_key_checking, and forks; privilege escalation uses become=True, become_method=sudo, become_ask_pass=True. The other options invent setting names (strict_host_key_checking, parallel, workers, escalate) that Ansible ignores silently — a classic source of 'my config does nothing' bugs.
scenarios.hint: Which of these key names have you seen in real ansible.cfg examples?

scenarios.title: The odd web server
scenarios.situation: All web hosts are RHEL at 10.0.0.x except web9, a legacy box at 192.168.5.9 reachable only on SSH port 2222 with a different user.
scenarios.prompt: How do you express web9's connection details in inventory without affecting the others?
choices: web9.example.com ansible_host=192.168.5.9 ansible_port=2222 ansible_user=legacy
Create a [web9] group with its own ansible.cfg file
Set the variables globally and override them back for web1–web8
SSH config can't help — Ansible ignores ~/.ssh/config
scenarios.why: Host variables are set inline after the hostname in INI inventory: ansible_host overrides the DNS name, ansible_port the SSH port, ansible_user the login. They apply only to that host. (Ansible does honor ~/.ssh/config too, but inline host vars are the direct, visible approach.)
scenarios.hint: Where can per-host connection variables live in an INI inventory?

scenarios.title: The playbook that ran on the wrong hosts
scenarios.situation: Your Ansible playbook patched the database servers instead of the web servers. The playbook header says 'hosts: webservers', but the inventory file your teammate handed you has a [webservers] group containing db01 and db02.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most reliable first step before re-running the playbook?
choices: Fix the inventory so groups match reality, then dry-run with 'ansible-playbook site.yml --check --diff' and limit scope with '--limit webservers' until verified.
Change the play header to 'hosts: dbservers' so the play matches the inventory as-is.
Re-run immediately with '-v' — verbosity will prevent it from hitting the wrong hosts.
Delete the inventory and use '-i db01,' inline host lists for every future run.
scenarios.why: The inventory is the source of truth for group membership — the play did exactly what it was told. Fixing group membership and validating with --check/--diff plus --limit contains the blast radius. Renaming the play header just re-labels the mistake; verbosity changes nothing about targeting.
scenarios.hint: The play targeted the group it was told to. Where does Ansible learn which hosts are in that group?

scenarios.title: One Command, Fifty Servers
scenarios.situation: You must check free disk space on all 50 web servers *right now*, without writing a playbook.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct ad-hoc invocation?
choices: `ansible web -m ansible.builtin.command -a 'df -h /'` — ad-hoc mode runs a single module across the inventory group immediately
Write a playbook; ad-hoc commands can't target groups
`ansible-playbook --check`; check mode runs shell commands
SSH into each server; 50 servers take 10 minutes
scenarios.why: Ad-hoc commands are Ansible's one-shot execution path: `ansible <pattern> -m <module> -a '<args>'`. The command/shell modules run the check across the whole group in parallel — no playbook file needed.
scenarios.hint: Which Ansible mode exists precisely for one-shot module runs?

scenarios.title: Anatomy of a first play
scenarios.situation: You write your first playbook to install nginx on web servers, but Ansible complains about the YAML structure. You mixed tasks at the wrong level.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct skeleton of a play?
evidence:
- tasks:
    - name: install nginx
      hosts: web
      dnf:
        name: nginx
choices: - name, hosts, become at the play level; tasks: as a list under them — hosts/tasks are siblings, not nested
Everything nests under tasks: — hosts and become go inside each task
Plays don't need hosts — Ansible guesses from the inventory filename
YAML needs tabs for the play level and spaces for tasks
scenarios.why: A play is a list item with keys like name, hosts, become, vars at the play level, and tasks: as a list beneath. In the broken example, hosts/dnf were nested under the task. YAML uses spaces (never tabs) with consistent indentation — 2 spaces per level is the convention. 'ansible-playbook --syntax-check' catches this fast.
scenarios.hint: Are 'hosts' and 'tasks' siblings, or is one inside the other?

scenarios.title: Don't shell out for this
scenarios.situation: A playbook uses 'shell: yum install -y nginx' and 'shell: systemctl start nginx'. It reports 'changed' on every run and fails when yum is replaced by dnf.
scenarios.prompt: What is the idiomatic rewrite, and why is it better?
choices: Use the dnf and service modules — they're idempotent (report ok when already correct) and abstract distro differences
Keep shell but add 'creates: /usr/sbin/nginx' to fake idempotency
Shell is fine — the changed status is just informational
Use the command module instead — it's idempotent by default
scenarios.why: Dedicated modules (dnf, service, copy, template, user, file) check current state and only act when needed — that's idempotency, the heart of Ansible. Raw shell/command can't know the desired state, so they always report changed and re-execute. Modules also handle cross-distro differences (yum vs dnf vs apt).
scenarios.hint: How does the dnf module know whether it needs to do anything?

scenarios.title: Restart only when needed
scenarios.situation: Your play copies three config files and must restart nginx — but only if at least one file actually changed. Restarting unconditionally on every run causes brief outages.
scenarios.prompt: How do handlers solve this?
choices: Each copy task 'notify: restart nginx'; the handler runs once at the end of the play, only if notified by a changed task
Add a service task with state: restarted after the copies — handlers are deprecated
Use 'notify' on the play — handlers trigger per task immediately
Handlers run before tasks, so put the restart logic there
scenarios.why: Handlers are tasks that run only when notified by a task reporting changed, and they run once at the end of the play (deduped even if notified multiple times). This gives you 'restart if config changed' semantics with zero outages on no-op runs. notify references the handler by name (or listen topic).
scenarios.hint: When does a notified handler actually execute — immediately, or later?

scenarios.title: Ten users, one task
scenarios.situation: You need to create 10 app users, each with a specific UID. Copy-pasting the user task 10 times works but is unmaintainable.
scenarios.prompt: What is the modern loop syntax?
choices: loop: over a list of dicts, referencing item.name and item.uid in the task
with_items: — the only loop construct Ansible supports
Write a shell for loop — Ansible loops can't set per-item UIDs
repeat: 10 with an index variable
scenarios.why: 'loop:' is the current standard (with_* are legacy). Looping over a list of dicts lets each iteration carry multiple attributes: user: name={{ item.name }} uid={{ item.uid }}. loop_control can rename the loop variable or add labels. One task, N items, full idempotency per item.
scenarios.hint: How do you give each loop iteration more than one value?

scenarios.title: Act on the previous result
scenarios.situation: You check whether /etc/myapp exists with the stat module, and only want to run the installer when it's missing. You also want the installer to report 'changed' only when it prints 'INSTALL OK'.
scenarios.prompt: Which task keywords combine to do this?
choices: register: the stat result, then when: not <var>.stat.exists on the installer, plus changed_when: "'INSTALL OK' in <var>.stdout"
ignore_errors: true on the installer — it will skip itself if the directory exists
failed_when: false — that converts failure into a skip
Use two plays — conditionals can't reference earlier tasks
scenarios.why: register: captures a task's result into a variable; when: gates execution on a Jinja2 condition (stat.exists is the standard existence check); changed_when:/failed_when: override how Ansible interprets the result. Together they give precise 'run only if needed, report honestly' behavior.
scenarios.hint: How does a later task see what an earlier task found?

scenarios.title: One line in sshd_config
scenarios.situation: You must ensure 'PermitRootLogin no' exists in /etc/ssh/sshd_config — replacing any existing PermitRootLogin line (commented or not) — across 50 servers, idempotently.
scenarios.prompt: Which module and arguments do this?
choices: lineinfile: path + regexp '^#?PermitRootLogin' + line 'PermitRootLogin no' — replaces the matched line or appends if absent
copy: with the full sshd_config content — simplest
shell: with sed — lineinfile can't handle commented lines
template: — but you must template the entire file
scenarios.why: lineinfile is built for single-line enforcement: regexp finds the target line (here optionally-commented PermitRootLogin), line: replaces it; if no match, the line is appended. It's idempotent — reruns report ok. copy/template of the whole file also works but couples you to the entire file's content.
scenarios.hint: Which module's whole job is 'make sure this one line is present'?

scenarios.title: The template that rendered nothing
scenarios.situation: A Jinja2 template deploys an app config. After a variable rename in group_vars, the rendered config silently contains empty values instead of failing. The service starts with defaults and misbehaves in production.
scenarios.prompt: How should the playbook be written to fail fast on missing variables?
evidence: ansible-playbook deploy.yml   # exits 0, config has empty values
choices: Reference variables with the 'mandatory' filter or set 'DEFAULT_UNDEFINED_VAR_BEHAVIOR' semantics via 'error_on_undefined_vars' so undefined variables raise an error instead of rendering empty.
Add 'ignore_errors: yes' to the template task so the playbook continues past the problem.
Wrap every variable in a default() filter with empty-string defaults to keep rendering stable.
Run the playbook twice; the second run fills in values the first one missed.
scenarios.why: Jinja2's default is to render undefined variables as empty strings, which produces valid-looking but wrong configs. Failing fast (undefined-variable errors, e.g. via the mandatory filter or error-on-undefined behavior) turns a silent misconfiguration into a loud, pre-deployment failure. ignore_errors and empty defaults hide the problem.
scenarios.hint: The template succeeded and the service started — that silence is the bug. What would make the render step refuse to produce output?

scenarios.title: Idempotence broken by a shell task
scenarios.situation: A role uses a 'shell' task to append a sysctl line to /etc/sysctl.d/99-custom.conf. Every playbook run reports 'changed', re-runs handlers, and your CI pipeline flags the job as mutating production on every run.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct idempotent fix?
evidence:
- name: Set swappiness
  shell: echo 'vm.swappiness=10' >> /etc/sysctl.d/99-custom.conf
  # runs every time, appends duplicates
choices: Replace the shell append with the 'sysctl' module (or 'lineinfile' with a regexp) so the task is declarative and reports changed only when the value actually differs.
Add 'changed_when: false' to the shell task so the run reports clean.
Add 'creates: /etc/sysctl.d/99-custom.conf' so the shell task runs only once ever.
Keep the shell task but run the playbook with '--check' in CI to suppress changed status.
scenarios.why: Appending unconditionally is inherently non-idempotent and duplicates the line each run. The sysctl module manages the key/value pair declaratively (file + runtime), and lineinfile with a regexp enforces one matching line — both report changed only on real drift. 'changed_when: false' lies about mutation; 'creates' prevents ever updating the value.
scenarios.hint: The task must converge: run it ten times and the system ends in the same state. Which modules are built to converge?

scenarios.title: Restart Only When Changed
scenarios.situation: A playbook rewrites the app config on every run and restarts the service every time — even when nothing changed. Deploys flap the service needlessly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct handler pattern?
evidence:
- template: src=app.conf.j2 dest=/etc/app/app.conf
  notify: restart app   # currently: command: systemctl restart app
changed=true on every run; restart on every run
choices: Use `notify` + a handler (`handlers: - name: restart app / service: name=app state=restarted`) — handlers run once at the end of the play and only when notified by a task that reported *changed*
Add `changed_when: false` to the template task; restarts stop
Run the restart with `ignore_errors: true`; failures won't flap
Handlers run on every play; use a shell `creates=` guard instead
scenarios.why: Handlers are Ansible's change-driven reactor: notified only by tasks that actually changed something, deduplicated, run once at play end. `changed_when: false` would lie about changes and break idempotency reporting.
scenarios.hint: What runs once at the end, and only if something changed?

scenarios.title: The Template With Logic
scenarios.situation: An Nginx config must list only app servers that are *not* in maintenance, from a group of 20 hosts with a `maintenance` host var.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct Jinja2 construct?
choices: `{% for host in groups['app'] %}{% if hostvars[host]['maintenance']|default(false) == false %}server {{ host }};{% endif %}{% endfor %}` — loop over the group, filter with a conditional, default the missing var
Write 20 static server lines; templates can't do conditionals
Use `{{ groups['app'] }}` directly; it auto-excludes maintenance hosts
Put the logic in a shell task; Jinja2 is for variables only
scenarios.why: Jinja2 in templates supports full for/if logic over inventory data (`groups`, `hostvars`) — the standard dynamic-config pattern. `|default(false)` guards hosts lacking the var; without it, undefined vars abort the template.
scenarios.hint: How do you iterate inventory and skip hosts conditionally in a template?

scenarios.title: Which value wins?
scenarios.situation: The variable 'http_port' is defined as 80 in group_vars/web, 8080 in host_vars/web1, and you pass '-e http_port=9000' on the command line. The play uses the default 80 from the role.
scenarios.prompt: Which value does web1 actually get, and what's the general rule?
choices: 9000 — extra vars (-e) beat almost everything; host_vars beat group_vars; role defaults lose to nearly everything
80 — role defaults are the most specific
8080 — host_vars always win over the command line
Ansible errors out on conflicting definitions
scenarios.why: Precedence (high→low): extra vars > task/block vars > role vars > play vars > host_vars > group_vars > role defaults. -e is the ultimate override (useful for one-off runs); role defaults/ are the weakest (meant to be overridden). Ansible never errors on duplicates — last/highest precedence silently wins, so know the order.
scenarios.hint: Which source is designed as the 'I really mean it' override?

scenarios.title: One play, two distros
scenarios.situation: Your fleet mixes RHEL and Ubuntu. The web package is 'httpd' on RHEL, 'apache2' on Ubuntu. You refuse to maintain two playbooks.
scenarios.prompt: How do you write one portable play?
choices: Use ansible_facts['os_family'] in a when: conditional (or a dict lookup) to pick the package name per host
Facts can't differ per host — split the inventory instead
Use the raw module — it auto-translates package names
Hardcode both names — the package module tries each
scenarios.why: Gathered facts (ansible_facts['os_family'] = 'RedHat' vs 'Debian', distribution, etc.) let plays adapt: 'dnf: name=httpd when: ansible_facts.os_family == "RedHat"'. Cleaner: a vars dict keyed by os_family. Facts are per-host truth — the portable-play mechanism. Disable with gather_facts: false only when you don't need them (it also speeds runs).
scenarios.hint: What per-host data does Ansible already collect that names the OS family?

scenarios.title: Building the server list
scenarios.situation: You need a comma-separated string of web hostnames for a config template, defaulting to 'localhost' when the group is empty, all uppercase.
scenarios.prompt: Which Jinja2 expression does this?
choices: {{ (groups['web'] | default(['localhost'])) | join(',') | upper }}
{{ groups.web.join(',').upper() }} — filters aren't needed
{% groups['web'] %} — print tags handle lists automatically
{{ groups['web'] | join }} — join defaults to commas and upper
scenarios.why: Jinja2 filters chain with pipes: default() guards the empty/undefined case, join(',') concatenates, upper transforms. {{ }} prints an expression; {% %} is for statements (if/for). Filters are the template workhorse — map, selectattr, to_json, b64encode, etc. Test expressions with 'ansible localhost -m debug -a "msg={{ ... }}"' (quote carefully).
scenarios.hint: How do you transform a value inside {{ }} without Python code?

scenarios.title: The load balancer needs all backends
scenarios.situation: Your haproxy config template must list every web server's IP. The template runs on the lb host, which doesn't know the web hosts' addresses.
scenarios.prompt: How does the lb host reach other hosts' facts?
choices: hostvars['web1'].ansible_default_ipv4.address inside a loop over groups['web'] — magic variables expose the whole inventory
Facts are host-private — copy them via files first
Use delegate_to: web1 — that shares facts automatically
Magic variables only work in group_vars
scenarios.why: Magic variables are always available: inventory_hostname (current host), groups (dict of group→host lists), hostvars (dict of host→all its variables AND facts). So '{% for h in groups["web"] %}{{ hostvars[h].ansible_default_ipv4.address }}{% endfor %}' builds the backend list. Requires facts gathered for those hosts (default behavior).
scenarios.hint: What variable holds every host's variables and facts, indexed by hostname?

scenarios.title: Organizing 200 variables
scenarios.situation: All variables live in one giant vars/main.yml. Web vars, db vars, and secrets are tangled; a change for staging once leaked into prod.
scenarios.prompt: What is the standard directory layout fix?
choices: Split into group_vars/web.yml, group_vars/db.yml, group_vars/prod.yml (+ host_vars/ for exceptions) — Ansible auto-loads them by group/host name
Put everything in the playbook — one file is simplest
Variables can't be split — Ansible reads only one file
Use -e for all 200 variables on every run
scenarios.why: group_vars/<group>.yml and host_vars/<host>.yml (next to the inventory or playbook) are auto-loaded per group/host — the conventional organization. Separate files per concern/environment prevent cross-env leaks, and vault-encrypted files (e.g., group_vars/prod/vault.yml) isolate secrets. Convention beats cleverness at scale.
scenarios.hint: What directories does Ansible automatically load variables from, keyed by group and host names?

scenarios.title: 'dict object has no attribute'
scenarios.situation: A template references '{{ db.primary.host }}' but fails on hosts where db_primary was never defined: 'AnsibleUndefinedVariable: dict object has no attribute'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the defensive fix?
choices: Use the default filter: {{ db_primary.host | default('localhost') }} — or ensure the variable is always defined
Wrap in try/except — Jinja2 supports Python exceptions
Ignore it — undefined variables render as empty strings
Delete the template — conditionals can't be made safe
scenarios.why: Ansible fails fast on undefined variables (a feature — silent empty strings hide bugs). The default() filter provides fallbacks: '{{ var | default("x") }}', and 'default(omit)' skips module parameters entirely. For nested dicts, define the full structure in defaults or use 'var.nested | default()' carefully — default only guards the last lookup by default.
scenarios.hint: Which filter supplies a fallback instead of failing?

scenarios.title: Whose Variable Wins?
scenarios.situation: A playbook sets `ntp_server` in three places: group_vars, host_vars, and `-e` on the command line. The deployed config used the wrong value.
scenarios.prompt: What is the precedence rule?
evidence: db01 got ntp2, everything else got ntp1 — the -e value was ignored?!
choices: Extra vars (`-e`) actually have the *highest* precedence — if the -e value was ignored, the variable is being redefined with `set_fact` or the play uses a different variable name; precedence order is: -e > play vars > host_vars > group_vars > defaults
group_vars always wins; that's the documented order
host_vars beats -e; extra vars are only defaults
Ansible picks randomly when a variable is defined twice
scenarios.why: The documented precedence (highest wins): extra vars → task/set_fact → play vars → host_vars → group_vars → role defaults. The scenario's surprise means something else redefined the var (set_fact/register) — knowing the order is how you debug it.
scenarios.hint: Where does `-e` sit in the precedence chain?

scenarios.title: From playbook to role
scenarios.situation: Your 300-line webserver.yml playbook is copy-pasted for three projects with small tweaks. You want to convert it into a reusable role.
scenarios.prompt: What is the canonical role directory structure?
choices: webserver/{tasks/main.yml, handlers/main.yml, templates/, files/, vars/main.yml, defaults/main.yml, meta/main.yml, README.md}
One big main.yml at the repo root — roles are just playbooks renamed
roles/webserver.yml — a single file per role
tasks/ only — the other directories are optional legacy
scenarios.why: 'ansible-galaxy init webserver' scaffolds the convention: tasks/main.yml (the work), handlers, templates/ (Jinja2), files/ (static), vars/ (high-precedence), defaults/ (low-precedence overridables), meta/ (dependencies, metadata). Convention lets anyone read your role instantly — and lets Galaxy/tools consume it.
scenarios.hint: What does 'ansible-galaxy init' create for you?

scenarios.title: Three ways to call a role
scenarios.situation: You see 'roles:' at play level, 'include_role', and 'import_role' in different codebases. They behave differently with tags and conditionals.
scenarios.prompt: What distinguishes them?
choices: roles: and import_role are static (parsed at playbook load — tags/conditionals apply oddly); include_role is dynamic (evaluated at runtime, respects loops/conditionals per call)
They're identical — pick by style
include_role is deprecated — always use roles:
import_role runs remotely — the others run locally
scenarios.why: Static imports (roles:, import_role) are pre-processed: the role's tasks merge into the play at parse time, so tags apply to all imported tasks and 'when' on the import applies per task. Dynamic include_role evaluates during execution — it honors loops, works with --start-at-task predictably, and is the choice for conditional/looped role application. Rule: dynamic behavior → include_role.
scenarios.hint: Which one is resolved when the playbook is parsed vs when the task executes?

scenarios.title: Overridable defaults
scenarios.situation: Your role hardcodes the nginx port in vars/main.yml. Users complain they can't override it without forking the role.
scenarios.prompt: Where should the default live, and why?
choices: defaults/main.yml — the lowest-precedence variable source, designed to be overridden by inventory/group_vars/play vars
vars/main.yml — it's already the right place; users should use -e
tasks/main.yml — define it where it's used
meta/main.yml — metadata is the override point
scenarios.why: Role variable precedence: defaults/main.yml (weakest — meant as overridable defaults) < inventory/group_vars/host_vars/play vars < vars/main.yml (strong, hard to override). Put tunables in defaults/, internal constants in vars/. Users then override naturally via group_vars without -e hacks or forks.
scenarios.hint: Which file exists specifically for 'sane default, please override me'?

scenarios.title: Reusing community roles
scenarios.situation: You need PostgreSQL and Redis roles. Galaxy has popular ones, but 'copy the tasks into my repo' feels wrong.
scenarios.prompt: What is the maintainable way to consume Galaxy roles?
choices: Pin them in requirements.yml and install with 'ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml' — versioned, repeatable, updatable
Copy-paste — vendoring is the only safe way
git clone into roles/ — requirements.yml is deprecated
Galaxy roles can't be trusted — write everything yourself
scenarios.why: requirements.yml declares roles (and collections) with versions/sources; 'ansible-galaxy install -r' fetches them reproducibly — like a lockfile for automation. Pin versions (or commit SHAs for git sources) so runs are deterministic. Evaluate Galaxy roles (downloads, maintenance, open issues) like any dependency.
scenarios.hint: What is the requirements file for Ansible roles?

scenarios.title: Role dependencies
scenarios.situation: Your 'app' role needs the 'postgres' role applied first on db hosts, and 'common' everywhere. You currently list them manually in every playbook.
scenarios.prompt: How do you encode this in the role itself?
choices: meta/main.yml dependencies: — lists roles to run before this one, with optional variable passing
tasks/main.yml — import the other role's tasks directly
Dependencies aren't supported — keep listing manually
requirements.yml — it also orders execution
scenarios.why: meta/main.yml 'dependencies:' declares prerequisite roles; Ansible runs them first (deduped across the play). You can pass vars to dependencies ('{ role: postgres, postgres_version: 16 }'). requirements.yml only installs roles — it doesn't order execution. Keep dependency chains shallow; deep chains become hard to reason about.
scenarios.hint: Which file in a role declares 'run these roles before me'?

scenarios.title: Collections vs roles
scenarios.situation: You need the community.postgresql collection's modules. A teammate installs it with pip.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct installation and usage?
choices: ansible-galaxy collection install community.postgresql (or via requirements.yml); reference modules by FQCN: community.postgresql.postgresql_db
pip install community.postgresql — collections are Python packages
Collections install automatically when referenced
Copy the collection into library/ — Galaxy is optional
scenarios.why: Collections (modules, roles, plugins bundled with namespaces) install via 'ansible-galaxy collection install' into configured paths (ansible.cfg collections_path). Use Fully Qualified Collection Names (namespace.collection.module) to avoid ambiguity as builtin modules moved into collections. Pin in requirements.yml like roles.
scenarios.hint: Which galaxy subcommand manages collections, and how do you reference their modules unambiguously?

scenarios.title: Role vs playbook sprawl
scenarios.situation: Your team has 40 playbooks, each 300+ lines, with the same user-creation, hardening, and package tasks copy-pasted everywhere. A security baseline changed and you must update all 40 files by Friday.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best structural fix?
evidence:
grep -l "Create deploy user" site*.yml | wc -l
40
ls roles/
(empty)
choices: Extract the repeated logic into Ansible roles (e.g. baseline, app_user) with defaults/main.yml, and have each playbook include the roles — one change then propagates everywhere.
Write a shell script that sed-replaces the baseline block across all 40 files.
Merge all 40 playbooks into one 12,000-line playbook so there is only one file to edit.
Copy the newest playbook's baseline block into the other 39 files manually for accuracy.
scenarios.why: Roles are Ansible's unit of reuse: tasks, handlers, templates, defaults, and vars packaged once and consumed by many plays. A sed sweep across 40 files is fragile and unverifiable; a mega-playbook trades duplication for unmaintainability. Roles with versioned defaults give a single source of truth.
scenarios.hint: The problem is duplication of logic across files. What Ansible construct exists specifically to package reusable logic?

scenarios.title: Don't Hand-Roll Chrony
scenarios.situation: Twenty RHEL servers need identical NTP config (two corporate servers, iburst, stepped once at boot). Hand-written templates drifted twice this year.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct RHEL-native automation?
evidence: 3 servers still point at pool.ntp.org from the old template
choices: Use the RHEL system role `timesync` (`ansible-playbook` with the `redhat.rhel_system_roles.timesync` role and `timesync_ntp_servers` vars) — vendor-maintained, idempotent, and the EX294-blessed path instead of bespoke templates
Keep the hand template but run it more often; frequency fixes drift
Use the `command` module to run `chronyc` directly; roles are overhead
Configure NTP once per server by hand; 20 servers is manageable
scenarios.why: RHEL system roles (timesync, selinux, firewall, storage...) are Red Hat-maintained roles encapsulating best practices — the exam and production both prefer them over bespoke config management. Hand templates reimplement (and re-break) what the role already handles.
scenarios.hint: What ships the vendor's own best practice as a reusable role?

scenarios.title: The Collection Maze
scenarios.situation: A playbook uses `community.general` modules but fails on a fresh controller with `couldn't resolve module/action`. It worked on the author's laptop.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct dependency handling?
evidence: collection installed manually months ago, forgotten
choices: Declare it in `requirements.yml` (`collections: [{name: community.general, version: '>=8.0.0'}]`) and install via `ansible-galaxy collection install -r requirements.yml` — in CI and docs — so every controller resolves the same content
Copy the collection directory from the laptop; vendoring by scp is fine
Rewrite the playbook to avoid community.general; only builtin modules are safe
Install with `pip`; collections are Python packages
scenarios.why: Collections are Ansible's distribution unit — requirements.yml + ansible-galaxy is the reproducible install path (and `ansible-navigator` execution environments bake them in). Laptop-only installs are the classic 'works for me' failure; pip manages Python deps, not collections.
scenarios.hint: How do you make a controller's content reproducible?

scenarios.title: Encrypting the DB password
scenarios.situation: Your playbook has 'db_password: hunter2' in plaintext vars. You need it encrypted at rest but usable by the play.
scenarios.prompt: What is the ansible-vault workflow?
choices: ansible-vault encrypt vars/secrets.yml (or encrypt_string for inline) — reference the variable normally; pass --ask-vault-pass or --vault-password-file at runtime
Rename the file to secrets.yml.vault — the extension triggers encryption
Base64 the value — that's what vault means
ansible-vault only encrypts playbooks, not vars files
scenarios.why: ansible-vault encrypt encrypts whole files (AES256); encrypt_string encrypts a single value inline ('db_password: !vault | $ANSIBLE_VAULT;...'). At runtime Ansible decrypts transparently with --ask-vault-pass (interactive) or --vault-password-file (automation — protect that file with 0600). 'ansible-vault view/edit/rekey' manage encrypted content.
scenarios.hint: Which two commands encrypt a file vs a single value?

scenarios.title: Two teams, two vault passwords
scenarios.situation: Team A and Team B share the automation repo but must not read each other's vault-encrypted files. One --vault-password-file can't serve both.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle multiple vault passwords?
choices: Vault IDs: encrypt with --vault-id teamA@prompt (or @file), and pass --vault-id teamA@... --vault-id teamB@... — Ansible tries each ID for each file
One password for everyone — separation isn't possible
Two separate Ansible installs — vault IDs don't exist
Encrypt everything twice — Ansible decrypts both layers
scenarios.why: Vault IDs label passwords: files encrypted with --vault-id teamA can only be decrypted when that ID's password is supplied. Pass multiple --vault-id flags (each @prompt, @file, or @script) and Ansible matches IDs to files. This gives per-team secret isolation in one repo — encrypt_string also supports --vault-id.
scenarios.hint: How do you label which password decrypts which file?

scenarios.title: Privilege escalation done right
scenarios.situation: Tasks need root for package installs but should run as the deploy user for app config. Some hosts use sudo, one legacy host needs su.
scenarios.prompt: How do you scope privilege escalation?
choices: become: true at play level (or per task), become_user: root default; override per task (become_user: deploy) and per host (ansible_become_method=su)
Run everything as root — scoping is overkill
become only works at play level — per-task isn't possible
Use the root user for the SSH connection instead
scenarios.why: become: enables escalation (default method sudo, user root); it works at play, task, or block level — set broadly, override narrowly (become_user: appuser for app tasks). Per-host: ansible_become_method=su in inventory. become_ask_pass / --ask-become-pass prompts for the escalate password. Least privilege: escalate only the tasks that need it.
scenarios.hint: At which levels can become: be set, and what does that imply for scoping?

scenarios.title: Secrets in the play output
scenarios.situation: A debug task prints the database password to the console log, which ships to a shared log aggregator. The task is 'fine' functionally.
scenarios.prompt: How do you suppress sensitive output?
choices: no_log: true on the task — censors its arguments and output from logs and callbacks
Delete the debug task — the only option
no_log only works on vault-encrypted variables
Logs are local-only — no action needed
scenarios.why: no_log: true prevents the task's args/results from being displayed or logged — essential for tasks handling secrets (even when values come from vault, the RESULT might echo them). Note it also hides output on failure (debugging trade-off — temporarily disable when troubleshooting). Apply at task or play level; it doesn't encrypt anything, just suppresses display.
scenarios.hint: Which task keyword censors output from logs?

scenarios.title: Key-based auth for 200 hosts
scenarios.situation: Password SSH to 200 hosts is slow and banned by policy. You need key auth with a passphrase-protected key, without typing the passphrase 200 times.
scenarios.prompt: What is the standard setup?
choices: ssh-keygen a keypair, ssh-copy-id to hosts (or provision via playbook), then ssh-agent + ssh-add to cache the passphrase for the session
Remove the passphrase — keys must be passwordless
One shared private key emailed to the team
Ansible can't use SSH keys — use passwords
scenarios.why: Public-key auth: private key stays local (0600), public key appended to remote ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. ssh-agent holds decrypted keys in memory after one ssh-add passphrase entry. For fleets, provision authorized_keys via Ansible itself (authorized_key module) — bootstrapping via initial password or cloud-init. ansible_ssh_private_key_file points at non-default keys.
scenarios.hint: What caches your decrypted key so you type the passphrase once?

scenarios.title: The vault password file
scenarios.situation: CI uses --vault-password-file /etc/ansible/vault-pass. It's currently world-readable. An auditor flags it.
scenarios.prompt: What are the hardening steps?
choices: chmod 0600 owned by the automation user, stored outside the repo; better: a --vault-id script fetching from a secret manager (Vault, cloud KMS)
It's fine — vault passwords aren't sensitive
Commit it to the repo for visibility
Delete it — CI should use --ask-vault-pass
scenarios.why: The vault password file is a master key: 0600, owned by the service account, never in git. The mature pattern is a vault-id script (--vault-id prod@/usr/local/bin/get-vault-pass) that fetches the password from a real secret manager at runtime — so the password exists nowhere on disk. --ask-vault-pass can't work non-interactively in CI.
scenarios.hint: Where should the ultimate secret live instead of a flat file?

scenarios.title: Password committed to the repo
scenarios.situation: A junior admin committed a playbook containing a database password in plaintext. The repo is internal but broadly readable. You need the password out of history and protected going forward.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct remediation?
evidence:
git log --oneline | head -3
a1b2c3d Add db password to playbook  <-- contains secret
grep -r "db_pass" group_vars/
group_vars/all.yml:db_pass: SuperSecret123
choices: Purge the secret from git history (filter-repo/BFG), rotate the exposed password, and store it in an ansible-vault encrypted file referenced by the playbook.
Encrypt the whole repository with ansible-vault so the committed password is now protected.
Delete the file in a new commit — the password is gone once the file is removed from HEAD.
Move the password to a README note saying 'do not share' and restrict repo access.
scenarios.why: A secret in git history stays in history until the history is rewritten, and anyone who cloned the repo already has it — so rotation is mandatory. ansible-vault encrypts variable files at rest; it cannot retroactively protect what was already pushed in plaintext. Deleting at HEAD leaves every prior commit intact.
scenarios.hint: Two problems: the past (history still holds it) and the future (it must be stored encrypted). One fix doesn't cover both.

scenarios.title: Vault password in CI
scenarios.situation: Your CI pipeline runs ansible-playbook against vault-encrypted variables. The vault password currently sits in a plaintext file on the CI runner, readable by every job on that host. Auditors flagged it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best practice for supplying the vault password in CI?
choices: Store the password in the CI system's native secret store and inject it at runtime via a vault password script ('--vault-password-file' pointing to an executable) or environment-backed script, with the secret scoped to the pipeline.
Commit the vault password file into the repo next to the encrypted vars so it's versioned with them.
Email the password to the team and have each engineer paste it into CI job definitions.
Remove vault encryption since the repo is private — encryption adds no value there.
scenarios.why: A vault password file that is an executable script lets Ansible obtain the secret from the CI secret store at runtime without persisting it on disk in plaintext. Committing it or emailing it defeats encryption entirely; dropping encryption removes the control the auditors asked for.
scenarios.hint: The password must reach Ansible but never rest on disk in plaintext. What mechanism lets Ansible ask for it at runtime?

scenarios.title: The playbook that won't parse
scenarios.situation: ansible-playbook fails immediately with a YAML error pointing at line 14, but line 14 looks fine to you.
scenarios.prompt: What is your debug workflow?
choices: Run --syntax-check to confirm, then inspect indentation around the reported line — YAML errors usually originate ABOVE the reported line (unclosed quotes/brackets, tabs)
Delete line 14 — the parser is always right about the location
YAML errors are random — rewrite the whole file
--syntax-check only works on inventories
scenarios.why: YAML errors surface where the parser gives up, which is often after the real mistake: a missing closing quote, mixed tabs/spaces, or wrong indentation level above. --syntax-check validates without executing. Also use 'yamllint' in CI. Remember: spaces only, consistent 2-space levels, quote strings with special characters (: { } [ ]).
scenarios.hint: If line 14 looks fine, where is the actual mistake usually?

scenarios.title: Preview before you wreck
scenarios.situation: You're about to run a playbook that manages firewall rules on 80 production hosts. You want to see exactly what would change first.
scenarios.prompt: Which flags give you a safe preview?
choices: ansible-playbook --check --diff — dry run showing per-task would-change status plus unified diffs of file changes
--check alone — diffs are automatic
Run it for real — previews are unreliable
--diff without --check — that previews safely
scenarios.why: --check = dry-run mode (tasks report what WOULD change; modules that can't predict may skip). --diff shows file diffs for template/copy/lineinfile changes. Together they're the pre-production review. Caveat: some modules don't support check mode well (command/shell always report changed) — know your modules.
scenarios.hint: Which flag dry-runs, and which shows file diffs?

scenarios.title: UNREACHABLE: 12 hosts
scenarios.situation: A playbook run shows 12 hosts UNREACHABLE with SSH errors, while 40 succeed. The failing hosts were reimaged yesterday.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause and the verification?
choices: Stale host keys (reimaged hosts have new keys) — verify with ssh-keyscan/manual SSH, then update known_hosts (ssh-keygen -R)
Ansible is broken — reinstall it
UNREACHABLE means the playbook has a syntax error
Increase forks — parallelism causes UNREACHABLE
scenarios.why: UNREACHABLE = couldn't even start the task (SSH/auth/network), vs FAILED = task ran and errored. Reimaged hosts → new SSH host keys → 'Host key verification failed'. Verify manually (ssh user@host), clear the stale key (ssh-keygen -R host), and accept the new one deliberately (TOFU with verification). Never blindly disable host_key_checking in production.
scenarios.hint: What changed about those 12 hosts yesterday that SSH cares about?

scenarios.title: Reading the failure output
scenarios.situation: A task FAILED with a terse message. You need the module's full stderr, the exact command run, and connection details.
scenarios.prompt: How do you get the details?
choices: Re-run with -vvv — shows task args, module invocation, SSH commands, and full result dictionaries
-v is enough for everything — more vs are decorative
Verbosity can't show module internals — read the source
Failures have no details — rewrite the task blindly
scenarios.why: Verbosity ladder: -v (task results), -vv (task input), -vvv (connection + module execution details), -vvvv (connection plugin debug). For failures, -vvv usually reveals the exact remote command and stderr. Combine with --step to interactively walk tasks, or --start-at-task to resume mid-playbook after a fix.
scenarios.hint: How many v's show the SSH command and full result dict?

scenarios.title: The 10-minute gather
scenarios.situation: Every playbook run spends 10 minutes in 'Gathering Facts' on hosts with huge NFS mounts and hundreds of interfaces.
scenarios.prompt: What are the optimization options?
choices: gather_facts: false (when facts aren't needed), gather_subset to limit (e.g., !hardware), or fact caching (jsonfile/redis) across runs
Facts can't be skipped — it's mandatory
Increase forks — gathering parallelizes per host already
Delete the NFS mounts — facts require clean mounts
scenarios.why: Fact gathering runs the setup module per host — expensive with many mounts/devices. Options: disable entirely (gather_facts: false) for plays not needing facts; gather_subset: ['!all', '!min'] trims categories; fact caching (ansible.cfg fact_caching=jsonfile, with timeout) reuses facts across playbook runs. Measure first: -vv shows per-task timing.
scenarios.hint: Do all your plays actually use ansible_facts?

scenarios.title: Proving idempotency
scenarios.situation: Your team requires playbooks to be idempotent. You need to demonstrate yours is — and find the tasks that aren't.
scenarios.prompt: What is the standard test?
choices: Run the playbook twice: the second run should report 0 changed (all ok) — any 'changed' on run two is a non-idempotent task to fix (often shell/command without creates/removes guards)
Run once — changed on first run proves idempotency
Idempotency can't be tested — it's theoretical
--check proves idempotency
scenarios.why: The double-run test is the idempotency proof: run 1 converges (changed expected), run 2 must be all-ok. Tasks still 'changed' on run 2 are the culprits — usually command/shell tasks lacking changed_when/creates, or template/copy with dynamic content (timestamps). Fix with proper modules, changed_when, or creates:/removes: guards.
scenarios.hint: What should the second consecutive run report?

Choose the newest technology — latest is always best.
Delay the decision — more analysis is always better.

choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Playbooks issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately

scenarios.prompt: What is the correct incident response sequence for this Ansible Collections degradation?

lessons.title: Inventory & Config — Core concepts
concepts: ansible.cfg: ansible uses the FIRST config found in this order: ANSIBLE_CONFIG environment variable, ./ansible.cfg (project), ~/.ansible.cfg (user), /etc/ansible.cfg (system).

Inventory structure: host variables are set inline after the hostname in INI inventory: ansible_host overrides the DNS name, ansible_port the SSH port, ansible_user the login. There is no --skip-hosts flag, and editing inventory for a one-off change is error-prone.
Parent/child groups: the :children suffix builds parent groups from child groups without duplicating host entries, so 'web' means every web server and 'boston' means every Boston host.
command vs shell: the command module executes the binary directly with no shell, so shell metacharacters (|, >, &&) are passed literally as arguments.

example.code:
[web]
web[1:8].example.com
web9.example.com
example.walkthrough: Host variables are set inline after the hostname in INI inventory: ansible_host overrides the DNS name, ansible_port the SSH port, ansible_user the login. They apply only to that host. (Ansible does honor ~/.ssh/config too, but inline host vars are the direct, visible approach.).

pitfalls: Common trap: list every host twice under literal [boston] and [web] groups with duplicate entries.
Common trap: ad hoc commands can't take arguments.
Common trap: put all hosts in one [all] group and use --limit with regexes for every run.
Common trap: remote_inventory=./inventory, trust_all_hosts=yes, concurrency=20, root=True.

lessons.title: Playbooks — Core concepts
concepts: Play structure: handlers are tasks that run only when notified by a task reporting changed, and they run once at the end of the play (deduped even if notified multiple times). A play is a list item with keys like name, hosts, become, vars at the play level, and tasks: as a list beneath.
YAML uses spaces (never tabs) with consistent indentation — 2 spaces per level is the convention.
Modules: dedicated modules (dnf, service, copy, template, user, file) check current state and only act when needed — that's idempotency, the heart of Ansible.
Idempotency: one task, N items, full idempotency per item.
notify: this gives you 'restart if config changed' semantics with zero outages on no-op runs. notify references the handler by name (or listen topic).

example.code:
- tasks:
    - name: install nginx
      hosts: web
      dnf:
        name: nginx
example.walkthrough: A play is a list item with keys like name, hosts, become, vars at the play level, and tasks: as a list beneath. In the broken example, hosts/dnf were nested under the task. 'ansible-playbook --syntax-check' catches this fast.

pitfalls: Common trap: YAML needs tabs for the play level and spaces for tasks.
Common trap: keep shell but add 'creates: /usr/sbin/nginx' to fake idempotency.
Common trap: handlers run before tasks, so put the restart logic there.
Common trap: conditionals can't reference earlier tasks.

lessons.title: Variables & Facts — Core concepts
concepts: Precedence (high→low): extra vars > task/block vars > role vars > play vars > host_vars > group_vars > role defaults. -e is the ultimate override (useful for one-off runs); role defaults/ are the weakest (meant to be overridden).

Facts: magic variables are always available: inventory_hostname (current host), groups (dict of group→host lists), hostvars (dict of host→all its variables AND facts). Gathered facts (ansible_facts['os_family'] = 'RedHat' vs 'Debian', distribution, etc.) let plays adapt: 'dnf: name=httpd when: ansible_facts.os_family == "RedHat"'.
os_family: cleaner: a vars dict keyed by os_family.
Jinja2 filters chain with pipes: default() guards the empty/undefined case, join(',') concatenates, upper transforms. {{ }} prints an expression; {% %} is for statements (if/for).
Filters are the template workhorse — map, selectattr, to_json, b64encode, etc.

include_role: dynamic include_role evaluates during execution — it honors loops, works with --start-at-task predictably, and is the choice for conditional/looped role application.

lessons.title: Vault & Security — Core concepts
concepts: Ansible-vault encrypt encrypts whole files (AES256); encrypt_string encrypts a single value inline ('db_password: !vault | $ANSIBLE_VAULT;...').

Vault IDs label passwords: files encrypted with --vault-id teamA can only be decrypted when that ID's password is supplied. no_log: true prevents the task's args/results from being displayed or logged — essential for tasks handling secrets (even when values come from vault, the RESULT might echo them).
Become: enables escalation (default method sudo, user root); it works at play, task, or block level — set broadly, override narrowly (become_user: appuser for app tasks).
Privilege escalation: least privilege: escalate only the tasks that need it.

lessons.title: How to Use This Red Hat Certified Engineer (Ansible) Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here (this domain: course overview, study strategy, key terminology) → Lessons (the deep-dives, in domain order) → Drills (practice scenarios, untimed, with full explanations) → Labs (hands-on exercises) → Mock Assessment (timed simulation). Each layer assumes the one before. Skipping straight to the mock burns your one realistic practice run.

What 'automation engineer' means in practice: this bootcamp prepares you for the real-world responsibilities of a automation engineer, not just exam questions. Every lesson connects theory to the decisions you'll make on the job — what to check first, what to try next, how to explain your reasoning.

The EX294 Red Hat Certified Engineer exam strategy: (a) first pass — read every lesson in order without skipping, taking notes on concepts that feel unfamiliar; (b) second pass — work every scenario and lab, reading the 'why' explanations even for correct answers; (c) final pass — take the timed mock under realistic conditions (no pauses, no references).

How to read the scenarios: every scenario has a 'why' explanation — read it even when you got the answer right, because it explains the WRONG answers too (and real exams design wrong answers from those same misconceptions). The hint is there to unblock you, not to give away the answer.

Active recall beats re-reading: after each lesson, close the page and explain the key concepts out loud in your own words. If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it yet — re-read that section.
Spaced repetition: revisit completed domains after 2-3 days. The bootcamp tracks your progress — use the dashboard to identify weak areas and drill those specifically before the mock.

example.code:
Week 1: Start Here + first 3 domains (lessons only)
Week 2: Remaining domains (lessons + scenarios)
Week 3: All labs + weak-area review
Week 4: Timed mock → review misses → targeted re-study
Exam/Interview: Confident and prepared
example.walkthrough: This 4-week plan assumes 1-2 hours per day. Adjust the pace to your schedule, but keep the order: lessons before scenarios, scenarios before labs, everything before the mock. The mock is a diagnostic tool — take it when you're ready to find gaps, not when you're still learning fundamentals.

pitfalls: Skipping the Start Here domain because 'I already know the basics' — the study strategy and terminology sections prevent wasted effort later.
Doing scenarios before reading the lessons — you'll memorize answers without understanding the concepts, and the mock will expose it.
Ignoring the 'why' explanations for correct answers — the wrong-answer analysis is where deep understanding comes from.
Taking the mock too early as a 'practice test' — it's a final validation, not a study tool. Use it once when ready.

lessons.title: Red Hat Certified Engineer (Ansible): Field Overview and Key Terminology
concepts: Red Hat Certified Engineer (Ansible) sits at the intersection of theory and hands-on practice. The professionals who excel are those who can both explain the 'why' and execute the 'how' under pressure.

Key terminology is the price of admission — every domain in this bootcamp assumes you can use the core vocabulary precisely. When you encounter an unfamiliar term, stop and learn it before continuing.
The field rewards systems thinkers: people who see how components connect, not just isolated facts. The Systems Anatomy domain teaches this explicitly — start there after finishing Start Here.
Documentation is a professional skill, not an afterthought. As you learn, practice explaining concepts as if writing a runbook — clear, sequential, with the 'why' for each step.

example.code:
Weak answer: 'I know about X.'
Strong answer: 'X works by [mechanism]. In practice, I've used it to [application]. The key consideration is [tradeoff].'
example.walkthrough: This is the answer framework for interviews and exams: mechanism → application → tradeoff. Every lesson in this bootcamp is structured to build this three-part understanding. Practice using it from day one.

pitfalls: Using jargon without understanding — interviewers will probe deeper, and vague terminology collapses under follow-up questions.
Learning tools before concepts — tools change, but the underlying principles persist across versions and vendors.
Neglecting the 'boring' fundamentals — advanced topics assume solid foundations, and gaps there compound.

lessons.title: Study Strategy: From Learning to Mastery
concepts: The learning pyramid: reading alone retains ~10%, but teaching someone else retains ~90%. After each domain, explain the concepts to an imaginary colleague — or better, a real one.
Deliberate practice: don't just re-read weak areas, actively test yourself on them. The scenario drills are designed for this — they force retrieval, not recognition.
Error analysis: every wrong answer is data. Log your misses by domain and concept. Patterns in your errors reveal exactly where to focus.
The 80/20 rule: 80% of exam/interview questions come from 20% of the material — the core concepts that everything else builds on. This bootcamp front-loads those in the early domains.
Sleep consolidates learning: study sessions followed by sleep outperform cramming. Don't sacrifice rest for extra hours — your brain needs downtime to build connections.

example.code:
Study session template (60 min):
  0-10:  Review previous session's key concepts (retrieval)
  10-40: New lesson + scenario practice (learning)
  40-50: Lab exercise (application)
  50-60: Write summary notes (consolidation)

End each session by writing tomorrow's starting point.
example.walkthrough: This template prevents the two biggest study failures: passive re-reading (no retrieval) and marathon sessions (diminishing returns). The 10-minute review at the start compounds over weeks — by exam day, early material is rock solid.

pitfalls: Cramming the night before — it produces familiarity (recognition) without recall ability, which is what exams test.
Studying only strengths because it feels good — the discomfort of weak areas is where growth happens.
No error log — without tracking misses, you repeat the same mistakes and can't measure improvement.
Isolation — discussing concepts with others (or writing about them) exposes gaps that solo study hides.

lessons.title: What Success Looks Like: Exam and Interview Readiness
concepts: Readiness isn't a feeling — it's measurable. You're ready when: (a) mock scores are consistently above the passing threshold, (b) you can explain any lesson's key concepts without notes, (c) scenario misses are rare and random (not clustered in one domain).
For exams: time management is a skill to practice. The mock simulates real timing — use it to calibrate your pace (e.g., if the exam allows 2 minutes per question, practice at that pace).
For interviews: prepare stories, not just answers. 'Tell me about a time when...' needs specific examples. As you work labs, note what you built and what went wrong — these become interview stories.
The night before: no new material. Review your error log, skim key concept summaries, and rest. Confidence comes from preparation, not last-minute cramming.
A automation engineer is expected to handle ambiguity. Exams and interviews test this with incomplete scenarios — practice making reasonable assumptions and stating them explicitly.

example.code:
Readiness checklist:
  [ ] All lessons completed with passing knowledge checks
  [ ] All scenarios attempted, error log reviewed
  [ ] All labs completed successfully
  [ ] Mock score above target (with time to spare)
  [ ] Can whiteboard core concepts from memory
  [ ] Error patterns addressed (no clustered weaknesses)
example.walkthrough: Go through this checklist honestly one week before your target date. Any unchecked item is a priority. If multiple items are unchecked, consider adjusting your timeline — rushing into an exam unprepared wastes time and money.

pitfalls: Confusing completion with mastery — finishing all lessons doesn't mean you're ready; the mock score is the real indicator.
Ignoring time pressure in practice — untimed perfection doesn't transfer to timed exams.
No interview stories prepared — technical knowledge without communication skills underperforms in interviews.

lessons.title: Capstone Project: Build Your Red Hat Certified Engineer (Ansible) Portfolio Piece
concepts: A portfolio project proves you can DO the work, not just answer questions about it. Employers and interviewers remember what you built far longer than what you scored.
Choose a project that demonstrates the full lifecycle: planning → implementation → testing → documentation → presentation. A automation engineer is expected to own work end-to-end.
Scope ruthlessly: a small project done well beats an ambitious project done poorly. Pick something you can complete in 2-4 weekends.
Document as you build, not after. Future-you (and interviewers) need to understand your decisions, not just your results.
Make it visible: GitHub repository with a professional README, architecture diagram, and demo instructions. If it's not on GitHub, it didn't happen.

example.code:
Project structure:
  README.md          # What, why, how to run
  docs/
    architecture.md  # System design and decisions
    setup.md         # Step-by-step build guide
  src/               # Your implementation
  tests/             # Validation that it works
  demo/              # Screenshots or video walkthrough
example.walkthrough: This structure signals professionalism. The README is your first impression — write it for someone who's never seen the project. The architecture doc shows you think before you build. Tests prove it works. Start with the README (write what you'll build), then implement.

pitfalls: Tutorial hell — following a guide step-by-step without understanding teaches nothing. Build something original, even if small.
No documentation — undocumented code is unusable code, and interviewers will ask you to explain your decisions.
Perfectionism paralysis — ship a working v1, then iterate. A deployed simple project beats an unreleased complex one.
Skipping the 'why' — every technical choice needs a reason. 'I used X because...' is an interview question waiting to happen.

lessons.title: Presenting Your Work: From Build to Interview Story
concepts: The STAR method for technical stories: Situation (context) → Task (your responsibility) → Action (what you did, specifically) → Result (measurable outcome).
Lead with the problem, not the technology. 'We needed to automate X because manual process took Y hours' is more compelling than 'I used tool Z.'
Quantify everything: time saved, errors reduced, performance improved, users served. Numbers make stories credible and memorable.
Prepare for deep dives: interviewers will pick one detail and probe. Know your architecture cold — every component, every tradeoff, every alternative you considered.
Show the messy parts: what went wrong, how you debugged it, what you'd do differently. This demonstrates maturity more than a flawless narrative.

example.code:
Weak: 'I built a thing with React.'
Strong: 'Our team spent 6 hours weekly on manual deployments. I built an automated pipeline using [tools] that cut deployment time to 15 minutes and eliminated config drift. The hardest part was [challenge] — I solved it by [approach].'
example.walkthrough: Notice the structure: problem (6 hours wasted) → action (built pipeline) → result (15 min, no drift) → depth (hardest part + solution). Practice telling your capstone story in 2 minutes, then be ready to go deep on any part.

pitfalls: Vague claims without specifics — 'I improved performance' means nothing; 'I reduced load time from 4s to 800ms by...' is compelling.
Only preparing the happy path — interviewers specifically ask about failures and challenges.
Memorizing a script — stories should feel conversational, not rehearsed. Know the beats, not the words.
No demo ready — always have a live demo, screenshots, or video. 'Let me show you' beats 'trust me.'

lessons.title: Beyond the Capstone: Continuous Growth
concepts: The capstone is a starting point, not a finish line. The best automation engineers are continuous learners — the field evolves, and so should you.
Build in public: share your learnings (blog posts, conference talks, open source contributions). Teaching solidifies your knowledge and builds your professional reputation.
Find your niche: general competence gets you hired, but deep expertise in a specific area makes you indispensable. Use the capstone to explore what energizes you.
Mentor others: explaining concepts to junior colleagues is the fastest way to deepen your own understanding and develop leadership skills.
Stay current: follow key practitioners, read release notes, experiment with new tools in a lab. Allocate 2-3 hours weekly to deliberate learning.

  Monthly: One deep-dive (new tool, advanced concept)
  Quarterly: One shareable output (blog, talk, contribution)
  Annually: One significant skill addition (certification, major project)

  Track: What did I learn? What did I build? What did I teach?

pitfalls: Stopping after the capstone — skills atrophy without use. Keep building, even small things.
Learning without applying — knowledge without practice fades quickly. Always pair learning with doing.
No community — solo learning is slower and lonelier. Find peers, join groups, contribute.

lessons.title: Handler Patterns
concepts: Handlers run once at the end of a play — even if notified multiple times

Handler names must match notify exactly — typos mean silent failures
Flush handlers with meta: flush_handlers when subsequent tasks depend on the restart

example.code:
tasks:

      src: app.conf.j2
      dest: /etc/app/app.conf

  - meta: flush_handlers  # Ensure restart before next task
  - uri:
      url: http://localhost/health
      status_code: 200  # Verify app came back up

handlers:
  - name: Restart app
    service:
      name: app
      state: restarted
example.walkthrough: The flush_handlers ensures the app restarts BEFORE the health check. Without it, you'd check the old (still running) instance.

pitfalls: Notify typos — handler never runs, config changes don't take effect

lessons.title: Execution Strategies
concepts: linear (default): each task completes on all hosts before next task — safe but slow
free: hosts race through tasks independently — fastest, but output is interleaved

forks = 20
strategy = free
pipelining = True

# strategy = mitogen_linear

pitfalls: forks too high — overwhelms the control node or target SSH daemons
free strategy with dependencies — tasks that depend on other hosts need linear

lessons.title: Inventory & Config: Performance Optimization and Scaling
concepts: Measure first, optimize second: profile Inventory & Config operations to find actual bottlenecks, not assumed ones.
The most impactful optimizations are often algorithmic (better approach) not micro (faster code).
Caching is the highest-ROI optimization for read-heavy Inventory & Config workloads — but invalidation is the hard part.
Scale horizontally when possible: stateless Inventory & Config components scale linearly; stateful ones need careful design.

example.code:
Optimization workflow:
  1. Baseline: Measure current performance (p50, p95, p99)
  2. Profile: Identify the bottleneck (CPU? I/O? Network?)
  3. Hypothesize: What's the root cause?
  4. Optimize: Change one thing
  5. Measure: Did it improve? By how much?
  6. Repeat or revert
example.walkthrough: Follow this workflow for a real Inventory & Config performance issue. Document the baseline, the change, and the measured improvement. If the change didn't help, revert it — don't accumulate complexity without benefit.

pitfalls: Optimizing without measuring — you can't improve what you don't measure.
Premature optimization — clean code first, fast code when profiling shows it's needed.
Ignoring the 99th percentile — averages hide the worst user experiences.

Security checklist for Inventory & Config:

  [ ] Authorization: What can they do?

lessons.title: Inventory & Config: Integration and Interoperability
concepts: Inventory & Config rarely operates in isolation — integration with other systems is where real-world complexity lives.
API design for Inventory & Config: version your interfaces, document contracts, handle failures gracefully.
Data format choices matter: JSON for readability, Protocol Buffers for performance, each has tradeoffs.
Idempotency: operations that may be retried must be safe to execute multiple times.

example.code:
Integration patterns:
  Sync (REST/gRPC): Simple, but couples availability
  Async (Queue/Events): Decoupled, but eventual consistency
  Batch (ETL): Efficient for bulk, but high latency
  
  Choose based on: latency requirements, coupling tolerance, failure handling.

pitfalls: Tight coupling — synchronous calls to unreliable dependencies cascade failures.

sections.heading: Inventory & Config
items: Inventory structure — host variables are set inline after the hostname in INI inventory: ansible_host overrides the DNS name, ansible_port the SSH port, ansible_user the login. There is no --skip-hosts flag, and editing inventory for a one-off change is error-prone.
Parent/child groups — the :children suffix builds parent groups from child groups without duplicating host entries, so 'web' means every web server and 'boston' means every Boston host.
Common trap — list every host twice under literal [boston] and [web] groups with duplicate entries.
Common trap — ad hoc commands can't take arguments.
Common trap — put all hosts in one [all] group and use --limit with regexes for every run.
Common trap — remote_inventory=./inventory, trust_all_hosts=yes, concurrency=20, root=True.

Host variables are set inline after the hostname in INI inventory — ansible_host overrides the DNS name, ansible_port the SSH port, ansible_user the login. They apply only to that host. (Ansible does honor ~/.ssh/config too, but inline host vars are the direct, visible approach.).

YAML uses spaces (never tabs) with consistent indentation — 2 spaces per level is the convention.
Modules — dedicated modules (dnf, service, copy, template, user, file) check current state and only act when needed — that's idempotency, the heart of Ansible.
Idempotency — one task, N items, full idempotency per item.
Common trap — YAML needs tabs for the play level and spaces for tasks.
Common trap — keep shell but add 'creates: /usr/sbin/nginx' to fake idempotency.
Common trap — handlers run before tasks, so put the restart logic there.
Common trap — conditionals can't reference earlier tasks.

Jinja2 filters chain with pipes — default() guards the empty/undefined case, join(',') concatenates, upper transforms. {{ }} prints an expression; {% %} is for statements (if/for).
Filters are the template workhorse — map, selectattr, to_json, b64encode, etc.

sections.heading: Roles
items: Role structure — you can pass vars to dependencies ('{ role: postgres, postgres_version: 16 }'). requirements.yml only installs roles — it doesn't order execution.

Static vs dynamic — 'ansible-galaxy init webserver' scaffolds the convention: tasks/main.yml (the work), handlers, templates/ (Jinja2), files/ (static), vars/ (high-precedence), defaults/ (low-precedence overridables), meta/ (dependencies, metadata).
